issues.legal_issue: Geographical differences in the protection given to tenants of non-residential buildings may justify treating towns differently when those differences are rationally related to the legislation’s purpose.
material_facts: The law retained protection for tenants of non-residential buildings in certain larger towns but withdrew it in other towns, including the town where the appellants’ leased sites were situated.

The retained towns had greater population, commercial activity and numbers of non-residential buildings; the Court found real differences between them and other towns relevant to the need for tenant protection.
The appellants challenged the differential treatment as lacking a rational basis.
issues.conclusion: The distinction between the specified towns and other towns was based on real differences and had a reasonable relation to the object of protecting tenants; it did not violate the guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: A legislative classification must rest on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the statute’s object. Classification may be geographical, and constitutionality is presumed subject to that requirement. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, Budhan Chaudhry v. State of Bihar and State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_legislation and (different_treatment_by_geography and relevant_differences_between_groups) and rational_connection_to_legislative_object

predicates.equality_challenge_to_legislation: A person challenges legislation on the ground that it treats comparable groups differently.
predicates.different_treatment_by_geography: The legislation gives different treatment to people or property according to the area in which they are situated.
predicates.relevant_differences_between_groups: The groups differ in circumstances relevant to the need addressed by the legislation.
predicates.rational_connection_to_legislative_objec: The differences between the groups bear a rational relation to the legislation’s object.

issues.definition: When legislation treats groups differently by area, a relevant difference between the groups that is rationally connected to the legislation’s object results in a valid geographical classification.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory option to apply for the purchase of land does not itself create a property right, and withdrawing that option before a sale is completed does not deprive the holder of property.
material_facts: The appellants were tenants of land on which they had constructed non-residential buildings.
They applied under a statutory provision for an order requiring the landlords to sell the sites to them at a price fixed by the court.
Before those applications were decided, an amendment extinguished the relevant rights and caused the pending proceedings to abate.

The appellants had not completed a purchase or obtained title to the land, and their constitutional claim concerned the statutory purchase option, not a claim for compensation under the separate provision concerning buildings.
issues.conclusion: The statutory right to apply for a purchase was not a right to property. Its withdrawal did not take away a property right or infringe the appellants’ constitutional property guarantees, so their request that the pending purchase applications proceed could not be granted. The Court did not decide the constitutional validity of withdrawing rights to compensation under the separate provision.
issues.legal_principle: The guarantee of property applies to concrete as well as abstract property rights, and a law depriving a person of property must be valid under the other applicable fundamental rights. But a statutory right to apply to purchase land is in nature no more a property right than a contractual right to purchase; it does not create an interest in the land before a sale is effected and title passes. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose, Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, Chiranjit Lal Choudhury v. Union of India, Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras and Maharana Shri Jayvantsinghji Ranmalsinghji v. State of Gujarat.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_withdrawal_o: A person challenges a law that withdraws a statutory option to seek the purchase of land.
predicates.statutory_right_only_allows_application_: The right granted allows its holder to apply for a purchase but does not itself transfer or grant an interest in the land.
predicates.no_completed_sale_or_title: No sale has been completed and the claimant has not acquired title to the land.

issues.definition: Where a constitutional challenge concerns withdrawal of a statutory purchase option, and the option has not resulted in a completed sale or title, the withdrawal does not deprive the holder of property.
